title: Word Search II
statement: Given an m × n board of characters and a list of words, return every word from the list that can be formed on the board. A word is formed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells — horizontally or vertically neighbouring — and the same cell may not be used more than once within a single word.
realWorld: The generic shape is 'match a whole dictionary against a stream or a space in one pass instead of one pattern at a time' — which is what intrusion-detection systems, content filters and `grep -F` with thousands of patterns do, using Aho–Corasick: a trie of all the patterns, plus links that let the scan continue after a partial match.

examples.explanation: "oath" runs o(0,0)→a(0,1)→t(1,1)→h(2,1); "eat" runs e(1,3)→a(1,2)→t(1,1). "pea" fails at once — the board has no 'p', so the trie has no such child at the root and the search never starts. "rain" runs out of adjacency.
a→b→c is not a valid path, and even reaching 'b' twice is forbidden: a cell cannot be reused within one word.
Duplicates in the input must not be duplicated in the output — clearing the trie's terminal flag on a hit handles this for free. "aa" would need the single cell twice.

constraints: board[i][j] is a lowercase English letter
words[i] consists of lowercase English letters
All strings in words are unique in the classic statement, but a robust solution should not depend on it

bruteForce.idea: Solve Word Search once per word: for each word, start a DFS from every cell and try to spell it out.

complexity.time: O(W · m · n · 3^L) — W words, each searched from every cell, each search branching three ways per step

bruteForce.whySlow: Every word is searched in complete isolation, so shared prefixes are re-explored from scratch. If the dictionary contains `oath`, `oaths`, `oat` and `oatmeal`, the path o→a→t is walked four separate times over the same cells. Worse, nothing prunes: a search for `zebra` on a board containing no 'z' still starts m·n times before failing. With W = 30,000 that is thirty thousand full-board traversals to answer one question.

patternIdentification: Two signals fire together. 'Search a grid for paths' is DFS with backtracking — mark the cell, recurse into the four neighbours, unmark on the way out. 'Match against a whole word list at once, not one word at a time' is the trie signal: the dictionary is fixed, the words share prefixes, and what you actually need at each cell is the question *is there any word that continues this way?* — which is exactly 'does this trie node have a child for this character?'. Inverting the loops is the leap: instead of walking the board once per word, walk the board once and carry a trie node alongside the position. The trie then prunes the search, because a branch dies the instant no word carries the prefix built so far.

optimized.idea: Build one trie from the whole word list. Then DFS from every cell, carrying the current trie node next to the current position: a step onto a neighbouring cell is legal only if the trie node has a child for that cell's letter. When a node is terminal, record the word stored on it and clear the flag so it is never reported twice. The trie turns 30,000 searches into one, and it prunes aggressively — most DFS branches die after one or two characters because no word continues that way. Store the whole word on the terminal node so no StringBuilder is needed, and mark visited cells by mutating the board in place, restoring the character on the way out.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to unmark the cell after the four recursive calls. The cell must be free for a different word starting elsewhere; leaving it as '#' silently loses matches, and the bug only shows up on inputs where two answers overlap.

Checking the trie after recursing instead of before. The child lookup is the prune — testing `child == null` at the top of `dfs` is what kills a branch in O(1); doing the work first and checking later throws away the entire advantage of the trie.
Re-walking the trie from the root at every cell. Carry the current node as a DFS parameter. Restarting means each step costs O(L) instead of O(1) and no pruning survives.
Rebuilding a StringBuilder path and looking each candidate up in a HashSet. Storing the word on its terminal node removes the string building, the lookup and the de-duplication in one move.
Reporting duplicates. Clearing `child.word` after a hit is the idiomatic fix and also handles a duplicated word in the input; a HashSet works but costs memory and hashing per hit.

Skipping the optional pruning of dead trie branches. After a word is found and its flag cleared, a leaf with no children can be unlinked from its parent, which shrinks the trie as the search proceeds. It is the difference between passing and timing out on adversarial inputs such as a 12×12 board of all 'a' with words like "aaaaaaaaaa".
Using `TrieNode[26]` without confirming the alphabet is lowercase-only — here the constraints guarantee it, but `ch - 'a'` on any other character indexes out of bounds.

Mutating the board and then returning it to the caller, or failing to restore it fully on an early return path. Every `return` after the mark must be preceded by the unmark, which is why the mark is placed as late as possible in the method.
